items.title: Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Pest-Surveillance Consortia Under Poisoned Extension-Device Reports: An Artificial Intelligence Governance Convergence Bound for Outbreak-Alert Reliability
items.abstract: Federated learning consortia that pool pest-surveillance reports from smallholder extension devices face a governance problem that is not captured by standard robust-aggregation theory: the adversary is not an anonymous network intruder but a ministry-level actor whose poisoning budget is set by administrative authority rather than by computational resources. The analysis is a replication-based design evaluation, not an observational study. Under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-four clusters were required for 80 per cent power at a 5-percentage-point effect. The governance convergence bound, not the statistical power curve alone, is the binding constraint on consortium design, and that the two must be evaluated jointly before an outbreak-alert system is certified.

items.title: Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated-Learning Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Cooperative Pest-Monitoring Under Adversarial Sensor Poisoning: An Artificial Intelligence Convergence-Guarantee Audit
items.abstract: Cooperative pest-monitoring networks that aggregate sensor evidence across farms through federated learning face a structural threat: a minority of compromised nodes can submit adversarial updates that survive averaging and corrupt the global model. Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are widely proposed as the remedy, yet their convergence guarantees rest on assumptions about update geometry that agricultural sensor deployments rarely satisfy. the present analysis audits those guarantees. It formalises the aggregation problem for a cooperative pest-monitoring federation, states the standard Byzantine-robust estimators (coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum), and derives the conditions under which each retains a bounded convergence rate under adversarial sensor poisoning. The audit shows that the guarantees are conditional on a contamination fraction and a heterogeneity bound that are not observable in deployment, and that the effective contamination fraction is inflated by non-IID pest phenology across farms. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) to show how many clusters a cooperative trial would need to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power: 52. Convergence-guarantee audits, not point accuracy comparisons, should govern the adoption of Byzantine-robust aggregation in computer agriculture.

items.title: Evaluation of Coalition-Formation Stability Bounds for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Advisory Councils Under Sequential Member Defection: A Governance Durability Estimation Strategy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence agriculture advisory councils are typically designed as standing coalitions of ministries, extension agencies, farmer organisations and technology providers, yet their durability under sequential member defection is rarely specified in advance. The analysis is a replication-based evaluation, not an observational study: no councils were observed and no defection events were recorded. Using a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design would require 52 clusters to detect a 5 percentage point defection effect at 80 per cent power. The before-after-control-impact estimator is a defensible durability bound only when the intraclass correlation is treated as a design parameter rather than a nuisance, and it specifies the conditions under which advisory council evaluations can distinguish genuine coalition stability from cluster-level heterogeneity.

items.title: Evaluation of Concept-Probe Sufficiency Audits for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Yield-Forecast Models Under Satellite-Revisit Sparsity: An Interpretability Reliability Bound for Smallholder Crop-Insurance Payouts
items.abstract: Concept-probe sufficiency audits are increasingly proposed as a precondition for deploying artificial intelligence yield-forecast models in smallholder crop-insurance, on the reasoning that a model whose internal representations can be decoded into agronomically meaningful concepts is safe to trust with payout decisions. The audit's inferential warrant is not intrinsic to the probe but depends on the temporal sampling regime of the satellite record that supplies the model's inputs. A formal reliability bound is derived for the sufficiency statistic under satellite-revisit sparsity, treating the probe's estimated concept alignment as a noisy measurement whose variance is inflated by the effective number of independent overpasses per growing season. The bound is then propagated to the payout decision through a before-after-control-impact estimator of the insurance indemnity, and the operating characteristics of that estimator are characterised under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The sufficiency audit's false-pass rate is governed jointly by revisit density and cluster count, that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80% power, and that the audit cannot by itself certify payout reliability below a revisit threshold that the bound makes explicit. The contribution is a reliability bound that converts an interpretability claim into a decision-theoretic one, together with the design conditions under which concept-probe sufficiency auditing is and is not a defensible gate for smallholder indemnity.

items.title: Evaluation of Concept-Probe Transfer Audits for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Cross-Regional Deployment: An Interpretability Generalization Bound for Smallholder Fungicide Safety
items.abstract: Concept-probe audits are increasingly proposed as a safeguard for computer-vision crop-disease classifiers deployed across regions, yet the audit's own transfer behaviour is rarely characterised. The audit is modelled as a two-stage procedure: a probe is fitted on source-region activations and then applied to target-region activations to certify that a safety-relevant concept, such as lesion evidence warranting fungicide application, remains decodable. A bound is derived that decomposes the target-region probe error into a source-region empirical term, a concept-distribution divergence term and a finite-sample concentration term. A before-after-control-impact design was used to characterise the audit's operating characteristics under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 design cells over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 56 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5 percentage-point effect. The bound implies that audit certification is a statement about probe transferability, not about classifier safety, and that smallholder fungicide decisions require the audit to be paired with an explicit divergence budget.

items.title: Evaluation of Constrained Coalition Formation Algorithms for Computer Agriculture Water-User Associations Under Heterogeneous Farm Sizes: An Artificial Intelligence Stability Bound for Participatory Irrigation Governance
items.abstract: Participatory irrigation governance depends on water-user associations whose members hold unequal land endowments, yet the coalition-formation algorithms proposed for computer agriculture typically assume symmetric agents or ignore institutional constraints on coalition size and composition. The analysis is theoretical and methodological: it specifies a cooperative-game representation of water-user associations in which farm size determines both water demand and voting weight, imposes institutional constraints on coalition membership, and derives a bound on the core stability of the resulting coalition structure as a function of the dispersion of farm sizes and the tightness of the constraints. The bound is then used to characterise the conditions under which algorithmic coalition recommendations remain stable against defection by large and small holders.

items.title: Evaluation of Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Computer Agriculture Land-Use Zoning Under Competing Tenure Claims: An Artificial Intelligence Pareto-Frontier Audit for Expropriation Risk
items.abstract: Agricultural land-use zoning in sub-Saharan Africa must reconcile competing tenure claims with productivity and equity objectives, yet the algorithms increasingly proposed for this task are evaluated almost exclusively on their ability to identify Pareto-efficient allocations. Pareto-frontier optimality is a necessary but insufficient criterion for zoning systems that allocate land under contested customary and statutory tenure, because a frontier can be efficient while systematically concentrating expropriation risk on politically marginal claimants. The framework is formalised as a constrained Markov decision process with a lexicographic constraint structure, and the audit is specified as a set of frontier-level diagnostics: constraint-violation density, risk concentration across tenure classes, and frontier stability under preference perturbation. No empirical data are analysed; the contribution is methodological and conceptual. The choice of constraint architecture, not the choice of learning algorithm, determines whether a zoning policy is tenure-safe, and that audits reporting only hypervolume or sparsity cannot distinguish tenure-safe from tenure-unsafe frontiers. The proposed audit provides a reproducible diagnostic that regulators can apply to any multi-objective zoning model before deployment.

items.title: Evaluation of Contestable-Explanation Sufficiency for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Loan Denials Under Appellate Bureaucratic Review: A Governance Reversal-Rate Estimation Strategy
items.abstract: Agricultural credit algorithms that deny loans must supply explanations that smallholders can contest before appellate bureaucrats. the present analysis treats the sufficiency of those explanations as a governance parameter rather than a technical property, and proposes a reversal-rate estimation strategy for evaluating it. The design is a before-after-control-impact (BACI) comparison in which appellate panels are observed before and after the introduction of a contestable-explanation standard, with untreated panels providing the counterfactual trend. Because no observational data are used, the paper characterises the operating characteristics of the estimator under a declared variance structure: between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5, and intraclass correlation 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage point shift in reversal rates at 80 per cent power. Reversal-rate estimation converts explanation sufficiency from an interpretive claim into a measurable governance quantity, and it specifies the institutional conditions under which that quantity can be trusted.

items.title: Evaluation of Counterfactual Audit Sampling for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Procurement Under Bid-Rigging: A Governance Detection-Power Bound for Tender Integrity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly procured by agricultural ministries to allocate subsidies, score grant applications and forecast harvests, yet the audit designs meant to detect bid-rigging in those procurements have not been evaluated for their detection power. the present analysis treats counterfactual audit sampling as a governance instrument and derives a detection-power bound for the before-after-control-impact design that underlies it. The analysis is a replication-based evaluation of the estimator's operating characteristics under a declared variance structure: between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, residual standard deviation of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells defined by cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 52 clusters to reach 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect. At 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, power at that effect remained below the conventional threshold, and the minimum detectable effect at 80 per cent power fell only slowly as clusters were added. The bound implies that counterfactual audit sampling, as currently constituted, cannot certify tender integrity at the cluster counts African agricultural agencies can realistically audit. The contribution is a governance detection-power bound that reframes audit sampling as a statistical design problem rather than an administrative ritual.

items.title: Evaluation of Delegation-Chain Collusion Attacks on Liquid Democracy Voting for Computer Agriculture Cooperatives Under Quorum Thresholds: An Artificial Intelligence bribery-Resistance Bound for Participatory Governance
items.abstract: Liquid democracy lets members of computer agriculture cooperatives vote directly or delegate their weight to trusted peers, and it is increasingly proposed as a governance layer for participatory decisions on shared machinery, water and data. The delegation graph that makes this flexibility possible also creates a vulnerability that direct voting does not have: a colluding coalition can purchase delegations along a chain and concentrate voting weight without ever buying a single vote on the floor. the present analysis treats that vulnerability formally. It models a cooperative as a delegation graph with a quorum threshold, defines a delegation-chain collusion attack as a coalition that acquires consecutive delegations to route weight toward a target proposal, and derives a bribery-resistance bound that states the maximum share of the electorate a coalition must control before the quorum threshold can be met by purchased delegation alone. The bound is expressed in the coalition's size, the depth of the delegation chain, the quorum threshold and the cost of acquiring a delegation relative to the cost of acquiring a direct vote. Quorum thresholds interact non-monotonically with resistance: raising the quorum can either harden or soften the cooperative against chain collusion depending on whether the threshold is met by participation or by concentration.

items.title: Evaluation of Differential Privacy Budget Allocation for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Yield-Prediction Models Under Cooperative Data-Sharing Consortia: A Governance Privacy-Utility Bound for Smallholder Participation
items.abstract: Cooperative data-sharing consortia that pool smallholder yield records to train artificial intelligence (AI) prediction models face a governance problem that is not resolved by technical privacy guarantees alone: the allocation of a differential privacy budget across participating districts determines both the statistical utility of the resulting model and the distribution of privacy protection among members. The analysis is theoretical and methodological. It formalises the consortium as a federated learning arrangement in which a central curator allocates a total privacy budget across contributing units, and it derives the utility loss of the pooled yield predictor as a function of the per-unit budget, the number of contributing units, and the heterogeneity of yield distributions across units. The central result is a bound showing that equal per-unit budget allocation is utility-optimal only when units are homogeneous in sample size and yield variance; when they are not, equal allocation produces a privacy-utility frontier that is dominated by a size-weighted allocation rule. The paper further shows that the governance choice of allocation rule, not the choice of privacy mechanism, is the binding constraint on smallholder participation, because smallholders in heterogeneous districts face the largest utility penalty under equal allocation and therefore the strongest incentive to withdraw. The contribution is a governance privacy-utility bound that connects differential privacy budget allocation to participation incentives in cooperative agricultural data consortia, and a set of allocation principles that consortium designers can apply without access to the underlying data.

items.title: Evaluation of Differentially-Private Federated Distillation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Prediction Under Cross-Silo Heterogeneity: An Artificial Intelligence Privacy-Utility Bound for Cooperative Data Sharing
items.abstract: Cross-silo crop-yield prediction in computer agriculture requires cooperative learning across farms, cooperatives and extension agencies whose data cannot be pooled because of privacy regulation, commercial sensitivity and heterogeneous sensing regimes. Federated distillation has been proposed as a communication-efficient alternative to federated averaging, but its interaction with formal differential privacy under cross-silo heterogeneity has not been characterised analytically. The analysis decomposes the generalisation gap into three terms: a distillation bias that scales with the disagreement between silo posteriors, a Rényi-differential-privacy noise term that scales with the number of distillation rounds and the privacy budget, and a heterogeneity term that grows with the divergence of silo label distributions. The bound predicts that under high cross-silo heterogeneity the privacy cost of distillation is sub-linear in the number of silos, whereas the utility cost of local-only training is linear in the number of silos, so that distillation dominates local training above a threshold heterogeneity that the bound makes explicit. The bound is illustrated against a random-effects synthesis of country-level associations between electricity access and under-five mortality across 24 African countries (pooled effect -2.19361, standard error 0.26513, 95% CI [-2.71326, -1.67395], I-squared 99.2%), which establishes the order of magnitude of between-silo heterogeneity that the theory must accommodate. The contribution is a formal privacy-utility characterisation that converts a design choice in cooperative agricultural data sharing into a computable threshold.

items.title: Evaluation of first aid guidance for dermal chemical exposure in Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) used in occupational settings
items.abstract: BackgroundSafety Data Sheets (SDSs) are widely used to guide first aid following occupational chemical exposure. However, the clarity and adequacy of SDS recommendations for dermal exposure remain uncertain.ObjectivesThis study evaluated the adequacy and clarity of first aid instructions in sub-section 4.1 of SDSs used in a biotechnology research workplace.MethodsFirst aid instructions in 45 SDSs were assessed against World Health Organization guidelines and peer-reviewed burn management literature. Key criteria included instructions on removal of contaminated clothing and accessories, irrigation procedures (duration of irrigation and source of water), wound care guidance, and recommendations to seek medical attention.ResultsFor chemicals capable of causing dermal burns (Category 1 skin corrosives), only 22% of SDSs recommended immediate removal of contaminated clothing, and 44% advised seeking urgent medical attention after irrigation. Although irrigation was mentioned in all SDSs, essential details such as irrigation duration, use of running water, and the role of emergency showers were omitted. Similar deficiencies were observed for chemicals associated with less severe dermal injuries.ConclusionsMany SDSs provide limited and nonspecific first aid guidance for dermal chemical exposure. Insufficient instructions may compromise early response to workplace chemical accidents and increase reliance on emergency medical services. Strengthening SDS guidance, together with enhanced occupational health training and involvement of occupational health professionals in workplace safety programs, may improve preparedness for chemical exposure accidents.

items.title: Evaluation of Gradient-Boosted Propensity-Matching Estimators for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Input-Subsidy Targeting Under District-Level Political Favoritism: A Governance Misallocation-Rate Bound for Smallholder Eligibility
items.abstract: The problem is that machine-learning targeting models are typically evaluated on predictive accuracy, not on the governance-relevant quantity: the rate at which subsidies are misallocated to ineligible households. A replication-based evaluation was conducted using 600 data sets of N = 500 drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). The ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under this process. The estimated bias for the intercept was -0.01261 and for exposure 0.00031; the root mean squared error was 0.84934 for the intercept and 0.01519 for exposure. Empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. A governance misallocation-rate bound can be derived from the sampling distribution of the exposure coefficient, and that this bound is more informative for subsidy targeting than conventional accuracy metrics. The contribution is a methodological framework that connects estimator behaviour to the political-economy problem of district-level favoritism, and a set of propositions about when gradient-boosted matching can be expected to reduce misallocation.

items.title: Evaluation of Mandatory-Human-Review Trigger Calibration for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Pesticide-Advisory Systems Under Regulatory Capture: A Governance Override-Rate Bound for Smallholder Safety
items.abstract: Mandatory human review is the principal safety valve written into proposals for regulating artificial-intelligence pesticide advisory systems in smallholder agriculture, yet the trigger that activates review is almost always specified as a fixed confidence threshold rather than as a governance instrument calibrated to the political economy of the regulator. It treats the override rate — the share of advisory outputs that a calibrated trigger routes to human review — as the object of institutional choice, and derives the conditions under which a trigger chosen by a captured regulator falls below the rate required to protect smallholders. The analysis is theoretical and methodological: no observational data are used or claimed. The bound is expressed as a function of the capture-contingent cost the regulator attaches to overriding industry-preferred advisory outputs, the smallholder safety loss from an unreviewed erroneous recommendation, and the base rate of high-consequence advisories. A trigger calibrated to minimise expected regulatory cost under capture is systematically more permissive than the safety-preserving trigger, and that the gap widens as the capture weight rises. items.title: Evaluation of Reprogrammable Prediction-Substitution Audits for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Subsidy Models Under Post-Deployment Retraining: A Governance Drift-Detection Bound for Smallholder Eligibility Stability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence models that determine smallholder subsidy eligibility are retrained after deployment, and retraining can silently alter which farmers are predicted eligible. the present analysis evaluates a governance instrument, the reprogrammable prediction-substitution audit, and derives a drift-detection bound for it. The audit substitutes model predictions for observed eligibility outcomes in a before-after-control-impact design, so that the estimand is the change in prediction-substitution error attributable to retraining rather than to secular change. Because no observational data are used or claimed, the analysis characterises the operating characteristics of the design under a declared variance structure: between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5, and intraclass correlation 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage point drift at 80 per cent power. The audit is a defensible governance instrument only when its detection bound is stated in advance and treated as a condition of deployment, and it specifies the institutional commitments that this condition entails for subsidy agencies operating under post-deployment retraining.

items.title: Evaluation of Temporal-Conformal Prediction for Computer Agriculture Pest-Risk Forecasting Under Phenology-Stage Shift: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Guarantee Audit for Insecticide-Timing Safety
items.abstract: Temporal-conformal predictors are increasingly proposed as a way to attach distribution-free coverage guarantees to pest-risk forecasts that inform insecticide timing, yet the guarantee is marginal over the calibration window and can fail when the phenology stage of the crop shifts between calibration and deployment. the present analysis treats the coverage guarantee as an auditable object rather than a property to be assumed. It formalises phenology-stage shift as a covariate shift on the stage-conditional risk distribution, derives the conditions under which split-conformal coverage degrades, and proposes a stage-stratified audit that reports coverage per phenology stage rather than in aggregate. The audit is demonstrated on a replication-based evaluation of a linear risk-score estimator with intercept, exposure, group and severity terms, using 600 replications of N = 500 observations drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). The estimator was characterised by ordinary least squares. Estimated bias was -0.01322 for the intercept and 0.00028 for exposure; root-mean-square error was 0.90474 and 0.01575 respectively; empirical coverage of the nominal 95% intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The audit shows that aggregate coverage can be satisfied while stage-conditional coverage is not, and that the gap is a function of the stage-shift magnitude and the calibration-stage composition. The contribution is a coverage-guarantee audit protocol and a formal statement of when temporal-conformal pest-risk forecasts remain safe for insecticide-timing decisions.

items.title: Every Alarm Has a Cause: An Open Generator of Telecom Alarm Storms with Exact Root Causes, Bound to NORIA-O, RFC 8632 and TMF642
items.abstract: Alarm root-cause analysis is studied on data that cannot be shared. Operator logs are confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types rather than per-incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent benchmarks carry per-incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a licence. We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of every alarm -- a by-product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted field binds to a term in NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines. A one-line rule -- rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm -- takes top-1 at 0.650 against 0.575 for our own temporal method, and wins 13 of 15 runs over three backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches 0.600, the same model allowed to query the graph 0.625, and the rule wins on real operator alarms too, at 0.773: a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that ranks alarmed devices scores 0.000 or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a silent candidate take 1.000 and 0.833.

items.title: Expanding the Occupational Therapy Workforce (1987–2001): A Qualitative Historical Study With Implications for the Future
items.abstract: Importance Documenting the origins, activities, and responses to the American Occupational Therapy Association's (AOTA) Multicultural Affairs Program (MAP) provides lessons that can inform future efforts to enhance workforce diversity. Objective Describe the need for enhancing diversity in the OT workforce during the 1980s and 1990s, articulate AOTA's strategic and programmatic responses to that need, and explore colleagues’ perceptions of MAP's work. Design We used a qualitative historical design. Primary sources were articles in OT Week (1987–1999) and OT Practice (2000–2001). Results The need for a diverse workforce was related to staffing shortages, enhancing the culture of the profession, and meeting clients’ needs. Data informed MAP's initiatives, which addressed recruitment, education, leadership, collaboration, and supporting organizational changes. MAP was discontinued abruptly in 1998 due to financial pressure. Colleagues valued MAP's work, as evidenced by attempts in 1999 to reinstate MAP and a report in 2001 requesting that AOTA develop infrastructure similar to MAP's. Conclusion and Relevance AOTA's MAP engaged in important data-informed programmatic activities which were valued by colleagues. Given that diversity and inclusion remain important priorities for the profession of OT, future efforts in these areas could build on previously used strategies. Impact Learning from past endeavors may enhance the sustainability and stakeholder engagement of modern-day efforts to improve workforce diversity and inclusion.

items.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
items.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence identifies circulating microRNA candidate biomarkers for liquid biopsy-based pancreatic cancer detection
items.abstract: Introduction Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains a highly lethal malignancy due to asymptomatic progression, late presentation, and lack of reliable minimally invasive liquid biopsy biomarkers for early detection. Circulating microRNAs (c-miRNAs) are promising clinical indicators owing to their stability in body fluids and regulatory influence on oncogenic pathways. Methods This study presents an integrated computational framework combining large-scale serum miRNA expression profiling with differential expression analysis, machine learning (ML), and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Five publicly available GEO datasets comprising 1,101 serum samples were analyzed through preprocessing, including normalization, missing-value imputation, and ComBat-based batch correction. A Bayesian stacked ensemble classifier integrating XGBoost, Random Forest, SVC, Naïve Bayes, and k-NN was optimized using SMOTE for class imbalance and constrained weight minimization via SLSQP. Results Gene expression analysis identified 148 significantly dysregulated miRNAs (|log2FC| ≥ 2, adj. p < 0.05). The model achieved excellent predictive performance (AUC = 0.97; accuracy = 97.28%; sensitivity = 94%; specificity = 99%). SHAP-based XAI interpretation highlighted 20 miRNAs as the most influential predictors, including hsa-miR-125a-3p, hsa-miR-1290, hsa-miR-614, and hsa-miR-497-5p. Pathway enrichment using DIANA-miRPath and miRDB confirmed their involvement in key oncogenic pathways (MAPK, CDK, TP53). Discussion As a retrospective computational study, these findings represent computationally prioritized candidate biomarkers requiring validation in independent external cohorts and experimental approaches before clinical application. The proposed pipeline demonstrates a transparent, reproducible approach for biomarker discovery and validates the clinical promise of circulating miRNAs in minimally invasive liquid biopsy-based early detection of pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Explainable Graph Neural Networks: Understanding Brain Connectivity and Biomarkers in Dementia
items.abstract: Dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with multiple etiologies, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and vascular dementia. Its clinical and biological heterogeneity makes diagnosis and subtype differentiation highly challenging. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently shown strong potential in modeling brain connectivity, but their limited robustness, data scarcity, and lack of interpretability constrain clinical adoption. Explainable Graph Neural Networks (XGNNs) have emerged to address these barriers by combining graph-based learning with interpretability, enabling the identification of disease-relevant biomarkers, analysis of brain network disruptions, and provision of transparent insights for clinicians. This paper presents the first comprehensive review dedicated to XGNNs in dementia research. We examine their applications across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and multi-disease diagnosis. A taxonomy of explainability methods tailored for dementia-related tasks is introduced, alongside comparisons of existing models in clinical scenarios. We also highlight challenges such as limited generalizability, underexplored domains, and the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) for early detection. By outlining both progress and open problems, this review aims to guide future work toward trustworthy, clinically meaningful, and scalable use of XGNNs in dementia research.

items.title: Explaining teacher adoption of AI through the technology acceptance model: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has accelerated rapidly, yet the factors shaping teachers’ adoption of these technologies remain insufficiently understood. A growing body of empirical research applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine how teachers integrate AI, focusing on perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and behavioral intention (BI). TAM was, however, originally developed for static, deterministic technologies, and AI differs in its opacity, adaptivity, and capacity to challenge professional roles and identity, raising the question of whether perceived usefulness and ease of use alone are sufficient to predict adoption intentions in this context. Following PRISMA guidelines, this study conducts a systematic review of 38 empirical studies ( $$N = 15{,}919$$ teachers across 19 countries) on teachers’ AI adoption, together with a meta-analysis of the subset reporting extractable bivariate correlations. A random-effects model (DerSimonian–Laird) is used to estimate the associations among PEOU, PU, and BI across $$k = 24$$ studies ( $$N = 11{,}768$$ ), while the full corpus is synthesised to identify contextual conditions shaping these relationships. Pooled correlations are positive and moderate to strong (PEOU–PU: $$r = 0.532$$ , 95% CI [0.410, 0.636]; PEOU–BI: $$r = 0.536$$ , 95% CI [0.435, 0.623]; PU–BI: $$r = 0.619$$ , 95% CI [0.511, 0.708]), and are robust to alternative variance estimators and to the inclusion of UTAUT studies under a construct-equivalence ruling. Heterogeneity is very high ( $$I^2 = 97.9\%$$ – $$98.6\%$$ ) and prediction intervals span from negative to near-unity values, indicating that these associations hold directionally but vary considerably across contexts in ways the core model does not represent. Egger’s regression indicates funnel asymmetry on all three associations; leave-one-out diagnostics attribute this asymmetry entirely to a single large-sample, low-effect study, and the asymmetry is not interpretable as evidence of publication bias under heterogeneity of this magnitude. The qualitative synthesis identifies five dimensions associated with variation in these relationships: AI literacy and trust as preconditions for usefulness judgments; a shift from functional to identity-based acceptance shaped by pedagogical beliefs and institutional norms; the role of sociocultural and institutional context; tool-specific adoption logics; and ethical risk calibration as a values-based gate on adoption decisions. These findings suggest that predicting teacher AI adoption intentions may require variables beyond the TAM core, and motivate the development of extended frameworks designed for the sociotechnical complexity of AI in education.

items.title: Exploring current practices in case-based discussion to enhance interprofessional learning in occupational health practice
items.abstract: BackgroundInterprofessional learning, particularly through interprofessional case-based discussion (CBD), can enhance interprofessional collaboration between occupational health professionals involved in the return-to-work of sick-listed workers.ObjectiveTo explore current CBD practices within Dutch occupational health practice and professionals' needs and anticipated barriers regarding interprofessional CBD.MethodsAn explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used, comprising a survey (n = 119), observation sessions (n = 3), and semi-structured interviews (n = 11) with occupational physicians, insurance physicians, and labor experts. The survey assessed current CBD practices, while observation sessions provided contextual insight. Semi-structured interviews offered in-depth understanding of current CBD practices and explored anticipated needs and barriers for interprofessional CBD. Interview data were analyzed using thematic content analysis. Findings were synthesized into a preliminary conceptual overview.ResultsCBD was predominantly conducted within monoprofessional groups. Overall, professionals were satisfied with their current CBD and valued the professional growth it fosters. Effective CBD was associated with skilled chairmanship, a structured approach, and a safe group atmosphere. Interprofessional CBD was expected to enhance mutual understanding and reduce distrust. Anticipated needs for interprofessional CBD included organizational support, a structured approach, and process-focused chairmanship. Anticipated barriers were primarily logistical, such as challenges in scheduling and information sharing. The conceptual overview suggests that interprofessional CBD can build upon existing CBD practice, but requires additional structural and process-related support.ConclusionsThis exploratory study provides initial insight into the anticipated value of (interprofessional) CBD for occupational health professionals. Results offer guidance for the future research on, and development and organization of interprofessional CBD within this field.

items.title: Exploring undergraduate experiences with AI tools in higher education
items.abstract: Purpose It aims to provide thorough insights into how undergraduates utilize, interpret and think about artificial intelligence (AI) tools in academic settings. Design/methodology/approach This mixed-methods study investigates undergraduate students' perceptions of AI tools in the classroom, focusing on both the perceived benefits and the concerns that arise from their use. Quantitative data were collected through an online survey administered to 107 undergraduate students, capturing participant demographics, AI tool familiarity and attitudes toward AI use in academic contexts. Exploratory factor analysis identified four key dimensions: perceived benefits of AI, attitudes toward AI integration in education, perceived challenges and concerns, and perceived impact on educational outcomes. These quantitative findings were complemented by semi-structured interviews with a subsample of participants, which provided rich qualitative insights into how students experience AI in practice. Findings The integrated findings highlight that while students are eager to leverage AI tools for academic advantage, they remain cautious about the broader implications. The study's findings offer actionable insights for educators and policymakers, emphasizing the importance of providing structured guidance, ethical frameworks and institutional support to ensure the responsible and effective integration of AI tools into higher education. Originality/value By investigating the perceived advantages, difficulties and educational effects of AI tools from the viewpoint of students, this study seeks to close that gap.

items.title: Federated Distillation Inference for Computer Agriculture Pest-Recognition Models Under On-Farm Data Residency Constraints: An Artificial Intelligence Communication-Efficiency Generalization Bound
items.abstract: On-farm pest recognition requires models trained across growers who cannot share raw imagery, and federated distillation is the standard architectural answer. Its communication cost, however, is usually treated as an engineering overhead rather than as a quantity that governs what the aggregated student can be guaranteed to learn. the present analysis derives a communication-efficiency generalization bound for federated distillation in which the teacher ensemble's soft-label agreement, the number of communication rounds, and the on-farm data-residency constraint enter the bound explicitly. The derivation treats the distillation round as a contraction of the student-teacher disagreement in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space, and the bound is stated as a function of the number of participating farms, the per-round communication budget, and the Rademacher complexity of the student hypothesis class. A design study characterises the operating characteristics of the bound under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The bound predicts that 52 clusters are required for 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage-point effect, and the design study confirms that the bound's communication term dominates the generalization gap at small cluster counts. The contribution is a formal statement of when federated distillation inference is communication-efficient in a sense that matters for generalization, not merely for bandwidth.

items.title: Federated Inference for Computer Agriculture Pest-Risk Prediction Under Cross-Farm Non-IID Data: An Artificial Intelligence Differential-Privacy Utility Bound
items.abstract: Pest-risk prediction across federated farms is complicated by heterogeneity in local data distributions and by the privacy guarantees required for sharing model updates. The analysis formalises the federated learning problem as minimising a weighted sum of local empirical risks subject to a Rényi differential privacy constraint, and derives a high-probability bound on the excess risk of the private federated estimator relative to the non-private oracle. The bound decomposes into three terms: a statistical term that scales with the number of farms and local sample sizes, a heterogeneity term that depends on the divergence between local and global risk minimisers, and a privacy term that grows with the noise multiplier and the number of inference rounds. The principal result shows that the privacy-utility trade-off is governed by the product of the noise multiplier and the square root of the number of rounds, and that this product can be controlled by early stopping without sacrificing the statistical rate. The bound is illustrated through a design-based evaluation using a before-after-control-impact estimator with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and residual standard deviation of 4.5; power was estimated across 2000 replications per cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The results indicate that 54 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5 percentage point effect. The paper concludes that differential privacy in federated pest-risk prediction imposes a quantifiable and manageable cost, and that the bound provides a principled basis for selecting privacy parameters in agricultural inference systems.

items.title: Few-Shot Transfer of Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Disease Classifiers Across Agro-Ecological Zones Under Label Scarcity: A Computer Meta-Learning Generalization Bound
items.abstract: Deploying crop-disease classifiers across agro-ecological zones is constrained less by model capacity than by the joint scarcity of labels in the target zone and the distributional shift between zones. The bound decomposes target-zone risk into three terms: the empirical meta-training risk, a Rademacher complexity term that scales with the number of few-shot tasks and the hypothesis-class capacity, and a task-divergence term that measures the discrepancy between source and target zone distributions. A before-after-control-impact design is used to evaluate the operating characteristics of the bound under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-two clusters were required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis is theoretical and design-based: no observational field data are used or claimed. The contribution is a bound that makes the label cost of cross-zone transfer explicit and a design analysis that tells practitioners how many zones, tasks and labels a credible transfer claim requires.

items.title: Flashcard creation and use in a histology lecture course: A survey-based case study.
items.abstract: Histology, like many basic science subjects requires mastery of terminology, visual structures, and integration of these things to describe functional relationships, making effective study strategies essential for student success. Flashcards are widely used to support retrieval practice and spaced repetition, but students can struggle to develop deeper understanding beyond surface memorization. The relatively recent integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mainstream higher education exposes new opportunities to enhance active learning strategies. This case study assesses the extent to which flashcards are being used by students in a histology lecture class, and explores the role that AI plays. Data were collected through two voluntary online surveys that included questions asking for multiple-choice responses and short written responses. The subjective and quantitative comparisons together with students’ self-reflection statements prompted classroom discussions about intentional flashcard design and use, and the broader applicability of course-specific study strategies.

items.title: Flat-RLVR: Sharpness-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Reasoning Capacity in LLMs
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly through group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), has emerged as a central paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs). While RLVR is highly effective at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, it commonly induces \textit{distribution sharpening}, whereby the policy distribution becomes excessively peaked and rare-yet-correct trajectories are progressively suppressed, thus diminishing sample diversity. To this end, we promote flat-reward optima in RLVR to smooth the policy distribution. We theoretically link flat reward RLVR to reduced distribution sharpening, and empirically show improved sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy. Our method, called \texttt{Flat}-RLVR, searches for flat reward regions via sharpness-aware minimization during LLM post-training, combining this with GRPO variants to achieve better trade-offs between sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.

items.title: From AI-Free Gates to AI-First Work: How Engineering Students in India Navigate University Education and Campus Placements Without AI Guidelines
items.abstract: Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026-2027, but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants' concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

items.title: From Artificial Intelligence to Institutional Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.

items.title: From Canon to Nikon: Camera Domain Shift and Potential Equity Implications in Retinal AI
items.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet access to regular screening remains limited worldwide. AI offers a scalable approach, but its performance can be sensitive to image quality and acquisition conditions. In a Brazilian cohort of 8,524 patients, retinal images acquired with the Nikon NF5050 were more than twice as likely to have inadequate image quality compared with those acquired with the Canon CR-2, despite refurbished Canon systems costing more than twice as much as Nikon systems. This potential cost-quality trade-off highlights an important consideration for the reliability of AI systems deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. Using a frozen pretrained retinal foundation model, we systematically evaluate whether camera-associated performance differences persist across 12 retinal disease classification tasks, four input resolutions, and five downstream classifiers. We find that camera-associated performance differences vary substantially across tasks, and that neither higher input resolution nor classifier choice consistently mitigates cross-camera variation. These findings identify camera platform as a potentially overlooked source of performance variability, with implications for the safety and reliability of retinal AI when deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. We release all source code, evaluation scripts, and per-task results on GitHub to support reproducible benchmarking.

items.title: From Code Scarcity To Verification Scarcity: The New Bottleneck in Agentic Software Engineering
items.abstract: I still remember how studying computer science felt in the early 2000s. Coding was a beast that overwhelmed almost everybody. Thinking computationally, then turning that thinking into syntax, was not an easy mental operation. We looked up to talented students who ranked in ACMICPC programming contests; they were known simply as the coders. After graduation, some of us even chose different tech careers just to avoid coding. For those who stayed, producing and debugging code could take weeks, and much of the development lifecycle was organized around waiting for it. Fast-forward to today, and AI agents can generate substantial amounts of code in minutes or hours. Yet many organizations still focus on how much more code or how many more features they can produce. Beyond that hype, a more important question is emerging: are we generating the right change, and will it remain right as the system evolves? The question, then, is no longer simply how much code we can generate, but how much software change we can generate while maintaining justified confidence that it is the right change. This article examines the emerging challenge of establishing that confidence as code generation becomes increasingly abundant.

items.abstract: This article examines the rise of Work-as-Imagined (WAI) and Work-as-Done (WAD) in New Zealand health and safety practice, using Maritime New Zealand v Anthony Michael Gibson [2024] NZDC 27975 as the local catalyst. It argues that Gibson should not be read as a narrow compliance case, but as an example of how officer due diligence depends on the organisation's ability to understand how critical work is actually performed. The article traces WAI/WAD through the evolution of safety and organisational learning, including scientific management, quality management, French ergonomics in the 1950s, Weisbord's organisational diagnosis, human error research, resilience engineering, Safety-II, and Human and Organisational Performance. It concludes that the practical task for officers, health and safety practitioners and representatives is to build disciplined ways to learn from everyday work before failure occurs.

items.title: FROM HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (HRM) TO ALGORITHMIC GOVERNANCE: THE CHANGING DISCRETION AND ROLE STRAIN OF LINE MANAGERS
items.abstract: Line managers once held wide latitude over hiring, appraisal, scheduling, and discipline. That latitude is narrowing. As organizations adopt algorithmic HR systems, decisions once anchored in supervisory judgment are increasingly pre-structured, scored, or overridden by software. This paper pursues two objectives: first, to examine how algorithmic management and HR algorithms reconfigure the discretionary authority of line managers across core decision domains; second, to analyze the role strain managers experience mediating between algorithmic outputs and the employees who live with their consequences. Drawing on an integrative review of recent empirical and theoretical literature, the paper finds that discretion is not simply removed but redistributed unevenly across recruitment, performance management, and scheduling, producing a manager accountable for outcomes they no longer fully controls This mismatch generates measurable strain: ambiguity about where authority sits, ethical unease about opaque scoring logic, and a residual burden of explaining decisions the manager did not make. items.title: From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet having more information does not necessarily mean understanding the world more accurately. From traditional storytelling and printed newspapers to television, smartphones and generative artificial intelligence, the ways in which people create, distribute and interpret information have undergone profound transformations. In From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Dawid Karol Kolodziej explores the psychological, educational and social consequences of these changes. Drawing on established media theories and contemporary scientific research, the publication examines why people believe misinformation, how repeated messages influence perceptions of truth, and how emotional narratives, cognitive biases and media framing contribute to the formation of individual and collective beliefs. Particular attention is given to artificial intelligence, deepfake technologies, synthetic media and the limitations of automated content detection. The author also investigates the relationship between AI-assisted productivity and independent human reasoning, considering how the delegation of cognitive tasks may influence critical thinking and information evaluation. A central argument concerns the unequal burden of information verification: while professional information producers possess considerable resources and influence, ordinary citizens often lack the time, expertise and technological tools necessary to independently verify every claim they encounter. The publication therefore challenges the assumption that combating misinformation should depend primarily on individual media literacy and emphasises the responsibility of publishers and information producers to substantiate factual claims and correct significant errors transparently. Building upon established scholarship, the author develops an updated five-dimensional conceptual framework for critical media citizenship, encompassing access and provenance, analysis of media construction and framing, evaluation of evidence and uncertainty, responsible creation and participation, and reflection on communicative power and shared responsibility. Combining social psychology, media education and critical analysis, this scholarly publication contributes to contemporary discussions about artificial intelligence, misinformation, public trust and the future of informed democratic participation. items.title: From Perception Errors to Unsafe Actions: A Survey of Behavioral Safety in MLLM Agents
items.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents connect perceptual inputs to tools and external actions, making safety a property of trajectories and retained state. This curated survey uses a constrained partially observable Markov decision process to organize six risk families: grounding failure, observation manipulation, miscalibrated authority, inference-time hijacking, unsafe commitment, and reusable-state corruption. We compare safeguards by mechanism, access requirements, and evidence scope, separating direct multimodal execution from transferred model-level and text-agent findings. The synthesis emphasizes image–text, GUI/web, and selected embodied settings; it is neither exhaustive nor independently coded. We distinguish response scores from executed violations and later-task reactivation, and propose containment and restoration outcomes for recovery evaluation. These distinctions motivate execution safeguards, calibrated autonomy, and integrity checks for reusable agent state.

items.title: From Policy to Practice: Collaboration, Inclusivity, and Integration of AI in Special Education
items.abstract: Abstract Special education is undergoing rapid change, as hyperspecialization and increasingly challenging needs are transforming the knowledge base and practices. School systems are implementing artificial intelligence (AI) policies, but most classrooms lack effective procedures, with a shortage of knowledge, competence, and willingness. The chapter starts with a qualitative synthesis of all known state and national policies in the USA to present an omnibus framework that results in the development of the ALERTS model: Adaptive and innovative, Learning and teaching, Ethics and access, Research cyle, Truth and accuracy, and Sustainability. The ALERTS framework considers AI implementation by stakeholder involvement and timing by planning, acting, and evaluating. The Contextual AI Roles (CAIR) model is presented as a model for implementing in special education at the three roles identified in the ALERTS framework. Specific recommendations for operationalizing the model framework suggest deciding roles of persons and AI, with solutions and possible problems. Inclusivity and maximizing outcomes are drivers in using AI in special education.

items.title: From Prompt to Performance in Tourism SMEs: Human-AI Orchestration and the Productivity-Capability Paradox
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) gives tourism small and medium-sized enterprises scalable cognitive and creative support, but access alone does not ensure sustained advantage. This conceptual article asks how firms can realize productivity gains while preserving the human and place-based capabilities required for future adaptation. An integrative, theory-building review connects tourism research with resource and asset orchestration, AI readiness, human-AI complementarity, organizational routines, and dynamic capabilities. Human-AI orchestration is proposed as a workflow-level configuration of task decomposition, contextualization, verification, and learning. Its contribution lies in coordinating established mechanisms rather than claiming that its dimensions are individually new. The prompt-to-performance framework distinguishes a capability-accumulation loop from a delegation-driven erosion loop. A proposed stock-and-flow mechanism explains switching between them: erosion dominates when losses from displaced practice and knowledge discontinuity exceed learning and replenishment; verification becomes vulnerable when retained capability falls below task-dependent requirements. Seven proposition families specify untested mediating, moderating, nonlinear, multilevel, and temporal relationships, with disconfirming observations. Sector-specific boundary conditions concern perishable service commitments, situated experience, partner interdependence, and concentrated expertise. Four configurations and a foresight matrix support contingent organizational choices. The contribution is a temporally explicit extension of automation-augmentation theory that separates immediate assisted performance from the evolving capacity to verify, recover, and adapt.

items.title: From Prompting to Engineering: A Research Agenda for Prompt Engineering in Software Engineering
items.abstract: Prompt engineering is increasingly used across Software Engineering (SE) activities, including requirements analysis, coding, testing, documentation, repository analysis, and planning. Yet prompts and related instruction artifacts are often created and evolved through task-specific and informal practices, with limited support for their systematic evaluation, management, traceability, and governance. To examine how SE can contribute to the maturation of these practices, we organized a structured community discussion at the First International Workshop on Empirical Prompt Engineering for Software Engineering (PROMPTSE), co-located with EASE 2026. Participants discussed current prompting practices, challenges to their adoption and evaluation, and future directions for integrating prompt engineering into software development. We synthesized these discussions into five areas: prompt artifacts and standardization; evaluation and benchmarking; lifecycle integration; human–AI collaboration and skills; and governance, privacy, and technical debt. Based on these areas, we outline a research agenda to move prompt engineering from predominantly ad hoc interactions toward more systematic, maintainable, evaluable, traceable, and governable SE practices.

items.title: From Sidq to Synthetic Speech: A Culturally Grounded Framework for Ethical Generative AI Communication in Arab Media and Public Relations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how organizations communicate with their publics. In journalism, public relations, and digital communication, AI systems no longer merely support content production; they participate in message creation, audience interaction, and reputation management. Existing AI ethics frameworks emphasize transparency, accountability, fairness, and privacy, yet offer limited guidance for communication practice in culturally diverse settings. This limitation is especially evident in Arab media environments, where linguistic diversity, cultural norms, and religiously informed moral expectations shape perceptions of communicative legitimacy.This conceptual article develops the SADIQ Framework, a culturally grounded model for ethical AI-mediated communication in Arab media and public relations. Through critical interpretive synthesis and normative comparison, it connects human-machine communication, communication ethics, AI governance, and contemporary Islamic ethical thought. It organizes the discussion around five tensions: speed versus verification, automation versus accountable agency, personalization versus dignity, optimization versus linguistic and representational justice, and engagement versus public benefit.The framework proposes five interconnected dimensions: Sidq and tabayyun (truthfulness and verification), Amanah (responsible stewardship), Dignity or karamah (privacy and human agency), Inclusive adl (linguistic and representational justice), and Qasd and maslahah (legitimate purpose and public benefit). All five apply throughout the communication lifecycle. Eight propositions, an organizational audit matrix, and an illustrative scenario specify a research and practice agenda. The contribution is an operational interpretation of ethical commitments for communication workflows; its effectiveness and cultural reception remain open to empirical testing.

items.title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
items.abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.

items.title: From tech-driven to principle-driven supply chains: responsible AI governance as a dynamic capability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in supply-chain forecasting, sourcing, planning, and logistics, yet governance arrangements required to ensure responsible use remain fragmented. This article develops a Responsible AI Governance (RAIG) framework that explains how ethical principles can be translated into operational supply-chain capabilities. Drawing on an integrative synthesis of AI-enabled supply-chain management, responsible AI, dynamic capabilities, relational governance, and socio-technical systems research, the framework connects three principles – transparency and traceability, validity and robustness, and role separation – to four mechanisms: model cards and explainability reports, data and model audits, responsible-sourcing clauses, and human-in-the-loop sales and operations planning reviews. These mechanisms are embedded in procurement, planning, scheduling, and logistics routines and are theorised to support agility, resilience, decarbonisation, and ethically legitimate decision-making. Six propositions specify the framework’s causal logic, while a 90-day implementation playbook translates it into managerial action. The article also develops frugal adaptations for emerging and humanitarian supply chains. Because the field is nascent and access to governance artefacts and data is limited, the study proposes a progressive validation agenda using simulations, vignettes, comparative cases, and micro-pilots. RAIG is positioned as a dynamic capability that turns responsibility from a compliance obligation into an adaptive source of performance.

items.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
items.abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

items.title: Future of Human Performance Modeling in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Toward AI-Augmented, Verifiable, and Agency-Preserving HPM
items.abstract: Human performance modeling (HPM) has historically converted theories of perception, cognition, and action into executable predictions for design. AI-mediated work now adds prompting, verification, tool switching, adaptive autonomy, and human–AI co-adaptation, creating tasks that fixed operator libraries and hand-authored models only partially capture. This paper introduces a framework for AI-Augmented, Verifiable HPM (AV-HPM), which keeps mechanistic HPM as the causal core, uses AI to accelerate model synthesis and calibration, and requires verification, uncertainty, stress testing, and governance before predictions are used in safety- or mission-critical design. We identify gaps in current practice, specify a layered architecture, and translate the framework into exemplar studies and minimum reporting criteria—a concrete agenda for making AI-era HPM scalable, auditable, agency-preserving, and cumulative across laboratories and domains.

items.title: GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality in e-commerce: the mediating role of perceived information overload and the moderating role of consumer involvement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support product search, comparison, and evaluation in e-commerce. However, consumers differ in their ability to use and critically evaluate GenAI-generated information, which may shape their perceived information overload and decision outcomes. Grounded in Information Processing Theory, this study examines the association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality, the mediating role of perceived information overload, and the moderating role of consumer involvement. Data were collected through an online survey of 401 Chinese college students and analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrapped mediation and moderation procedures. The results show that GenAI literacy is positively associated with perceived decision quality and negatively associated with perceived information overload. Perceived information overload is negatively associated with perceived decision quality and accounts for a significant indirect association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality. Consumer involvement further moderates the association between GenAI literacy and perceived information overload: the negative association is stronger at higher levels of involvement. These findings support an information-processing account in which consumers’ GenAI-related capabilities and motivational involvement jointly shape their perceptions of cognitive burden and decision quality. The study highlights the importance of strengthening consumers’ critical GenAI literacy and adapting AI-supported information presentation to different levels of consumer involvement.

items.title: Gender, Sexual Orientation, and the One-Year Refugee Bar: A Computational Study of Bill C-12 and Canadian Refugee Adjudication
items.abstract: In March 2026, Bill C-12 amended the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to make refugee claims ineligible for referral to the Refugee Protection Division where they are made more than one year after the claimant's first entry to Canada. Affected claimants are diverted to a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA), which is typically decided by an immigration officer on a paper record, with no guaranteed oral hearing, no appeal on the merits, and no automatic stay of removal pending judicial review. The government defended the bar partly on the premise that genuine refugees claim promptly. Critics countered that late claims are concentrated among vulnerable groups, particularly people fleeing persecution based on gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (SOGIE). This article tests those competing premises. Using artificial intelligence tools, checked through human review, it examines nearly 29,000 published decisions of the Refugee Protection Division, the Refugee Appeal Division, and the Federal Court from 2006 to 2025. The results of this study demonstrate that, first, while most claimants claim within a year, roughly one in nine in the published record does not, and gender and SOGIE claims are significantly overrepresented among these late claims. Second, among late claims, refusals of gender and SOGIE claims are more likely than refusals of other claims to be overturned on appeal or judicial review. Late claims on other grounds, by contrast, fare somewhat worse on review than timely claims. The one-year bar therefore removes the hearing, the appeal, and the stay from the late claimants for whom those safeguards have been doing the most work. The article recommends repealing the bar or, failing that, adopting exemptions, procedural protections, and greater transparency in PRRA decision making.
